newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Annan urges S.Africa to help Africa find peace.
newsitem.headline: Annan urges S.Africa to help Africa find peace.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan began his first official visit to Africa on Wednesday, promising his personal backing for peace in Zaire and Angola and urging South Africa to do its share to end regional conflict.
Annan arrived in Cape Town on a scheduled flight from the United States and was due to meet President Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who heads a post-apartheid truth commission.

Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told reporters it was significant that Annan had come first to South Africa, adding: "This visit will be fundamentally important not only for South Africa, but for Africa as a whole."

Annan's three-day visit could bolster South Africa's growing political and economic influence and fuel the African renaissance being promoted by Mandela and his hier apparent, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki.
"I think South Africa has a major role to play...in peace making and negotiations and helping to resolve conflicts around the African continent," Annan told reporters on his arrival.

"In time, I hope you will be able to participate in peace-keeping operations. I also expect that the voice of South Africa will be heard in the UN and other international fora on important issues of the day."
He said the priority was for Africa to settle its conflicts and shed its image as a continent in crisis.
"Africa cannot recover economically and socially unless we can resolve some of these political conflicts," he said.
His visit follows Mandela's inconclusive personal effort earlier this month to bring the warring factions in Zaire together for peace talks in Cape Town.
Mbeki represented Mandela at a summit of African leaders, excluding rebel chief Laurent Kabila, in Nairobi on Wednesday to discuss the burgeoning civil war in neighbouring Zaire.
Annan said he hoped the summit would consolidate the peace process and said he would personally participate in a second summit planned in Lome, Togo, on March 26.
He said he was told as he left the United States that a hitch had arisen in the formation next week of an Angolan government of national unity.
The U.N. chief, a native of Ghana, said he would go to Angola after South Africa to encourage the government and Jonas Savimbi's UNITA to settle their differences and start working together.
A 1994 peace agreement ended Angola's 19-year civil war, but the two sides have failed to set up the government of national unity envisaged in the peace accord.
Angola hosts the U.N.'s largest peacekeeping mission of around 7,000 members.

"I hope it will be possible that a national unity government will be formed during my visit to Angola. The people of Angola deserve it, they are tired of war and their leaders have to have the courage to give them peace," Annan said.
He said South Africa's peaceful transition from white rule to democracy should set an example for Africa, adding:

"There are difficult crises around the continent, but there is also good news. When we look at what happened here in South Africa...it reminds me of the great African capacity for forgiveness and for reconciliation."
